title: Bank One, N.A. v. Coates
lead: A satellite buyer challenged an arbitration amendment to his credit agreement while the bank sought a separate federal order enforcing it.

actors.name: Sky Scanner Satellite
actors.role: Other defendant that removed the original state suit

actors.name: S. Broadwater
actors.role: Local participant Coates sought to join

actors.name: National Arbitration Forum
actors.role: Designated administrator under the amended agreement

proceedings: State financing suit filed October 1999; another defendant removed it, and it was remanded August 2000.
Bank One filed this separate diversity action in September 2000.
District court: denied joinder, dismissal, abstention, and discovery; compelled arbitration January 2, 2001.
limits: The actual case involved satellite financing, while the assigned problem adapts it to deposit accounts. The opinion applies its 2001 arbitration authorities and historical Forum procedures, not a present-law or current-provider certification.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A signed credit application authorizes amendments
sections.cue: Begin with the actual financing agreement and notice.
paragraphs: Coates financed a home satellite system through a Bank One revolving credit-card plan. Immediately above his signature, the application said he agreed to follow the Account Agreement and Disclosure Statement issued from time to time. That agreement chose Ohio law and allowed the bank to change its terms with fifteen days’ prior written notice if required by law. A following sentence described how changed fees, rates, and minimum payments could apply to outstanding balances and future transactions.

On March 8, 1998, Bank One sent notice adding arbitration effective April 15. It covered claims arising from or relating to the agreement or account, including validity and applicability disputes, against either party and specified employees, agents, or assigns. It designated the National Arbitration Forum and its code, provided a hearing in the federal district containing the billing address, invoked the Federal Arbitration Act, and expressly warned that claims otherwise brought in court or representative litigation would require arbitration.

A customer could reject by mailing identifying account information by April 15 and continue paying existing balances under prior terms. Coates did not reject. He did not dispute the contract and notice facts or the clause’s coverage of his claims, but said he had never agreed to arbitration and that it was unenforceable.

sections.title: A state financing suit and a separate federal arbitration action follow
sections.cue: Keep the two routes into federal court distinct.
paragraphs: On October 20, 1999, Coates and thirty-seven other buyers sued Bank One and other defendants in Mississippi’s Bolivar County circuit court over the purchases and alleged improper financing. On November 22, before service on any defendant, Sky Scanner Satellite voluntarily appeared and removed to the Northern District of Mississippi, invoking federal statutes including the Truth in Lending Act. Bank One did not remove. It was served May 1, 2000, and answered June 2. Judge Neal Biggers remanded the action on August 23.

On September 7, Bank One brought this separate action against Coates under § 4 of the Federal Arbitration Act and identical actions against the other state plaintiffs. The state plaintiffs later sought a trial date, and the state court directed mediation. Coates asked federal Chief Judge Tom S. Lee to abstain, to join additional parties including local agent or employee S. Broadwater and dismiss for lost diversity, or to permit discovery before deciding arbitration.

sections.title: The narrower arbitration dispute has its own jurisdictional basis
sections.cue: Explain why joinder and parallel proceedings did not require dismissal.
paragraphs: The Federal Arbitration Act authorized enforcement but supplied no independent federal jurisdiction. The parties accepted that federal-question jurisdiction was absent in light of the earlier remand, but Bank One’s Ohio citizenship, Coates’s Mississippi citizenship, and more than $75,000 in controversy supplied diversity.

Lee rejected compulsory joinder under Rule 19. This action asked only whether Bank One and Coates had to arbitrate claims between themselves. Other alleged joint tortfeasors could remain in state court without becoming indispensable here. Coates’s joinder and consequential dismissal requests therefore failed.

The exceptional-circumstances abstention principles of Colorado River and Moses H. Cone favored exercising jurisdiction. Neither court controlled property; both were in Mississippi; convenience did not favor surrender. Piecemeal proceedings did not override the arbitration statute’s willingness to separate arbitrable and nonarbitrable disputes. The state suit’s earlier filing and trial-setting request were not decisive. Federal arbitration rules mattered, and an adequate state forum was not itself reason to abandon federal jurisdiction. Lee considered relative progress and the then-existing uncertainty about state-court enforcement under § 4. The factors supplied no clear justification for abstention. The failed removal by a different defendant did not make this a repeat of Bank One’s own unsuccessful jurisdictional effort.

sections.title: The documents permit decision without the requested discovery
sections.cue: Separate contract formation from allegations about the sale.
paragraphs: Lee applied the inquiry into a valid agreement, coverage, and any external legal obstacle, recognizing generally applicable contract defenses under § 2. Ohio law required both procedural and substantive unconscionability. A genuine making-of-agreement dispute could require trial under § 4, but an unsupported denial of assent did not create one.

Coates sought discovery about his agreement and arbitration’s costs and procedures. Lee found the relevant documents available, Coates’s own knowledge ascertainable from him, and incorporated Forum rules obtainable without discovery. The statute contemplated a restricted, expeditious inquiry. A mutuality or consideration topic mentioned in the motion was not developed as a substantive defense; Lee found no demonstrated defect and cited Ohio authority permitting modification without separate consideration unless required.

Coates’s affidavit alleged that the salesperson never told him he was signing for a Bank One credit card. Applying Prima Paint, the Supreme Court’s distinction between fraud concerning an overall contract and fraud specific to arbitration, and the Fifth Circuit’s R. M. Perez decision, Lee sent that overall procurement challenge to arbitration even though Coates called it fraud in the factum. The opinion made a similar clause-specific distinction for coercion and duress. It did not find that the salesperson actually committed fraud.

sections.title: The amendment power and meaningful rejection opportunity establish assent
sections.cue: Follow the court’s reading of this particular record.
paragraphs: Lee read the original amendment clause broadly. Its second sentence about specified financial changes explained their operation, rather than limiting the first sentence’s authority to amend other terms. Ohio banking law permitted the parties to agree to amendments, and the signed application incorporated this agreement.

The notice addressed arbitration alone, prominently warned of its effect, and explained rejection. Coates did not specifically deny receipt, although he did not recall it. Arbitration had not been hidden among unrelated changes. Small but consistent and legible print did not establish procedural unconscionability, particularly with a meaningful chance to retain the previous terms.

The court compared other banking-amendment decisions, including Badie and Long, by their agreement language, notices, and, in Long, a distinct retroactivity issue. It did not treat silence as free-standing assent divorced from the existing amendment power. Nor did a valid arbitration agreement require a separate clear and unmistakable Seventh Amendment waiver: moving the covered dispute to arbitration necessarily removed its judicial jury trial. That reasoning followed, rather than replaced, the formation analysis.

sections.title: The historical arbitration procedures do not establish unconscionability
sections.cue: End with the remaining objections and exact order.
paragraphs: Coates asserted prohibitive expense, inadequate remedies, and bias. The incorporated Forum code allowed substantive-law remedies, including attorney’s fees where authorized, injunctive relief, and a requested written opinion. Small claims had relatively modest filing and administrative fees; indigent consumers could seek relief; arbitrators could shift a prevailing party’s fees. Under Green Tree Financial v. Randolph, the Supreme Court’s arbitration-cost decision, Coates needed to establish likely prohibitive expense rather than merely assert it. The discussion of Justice Ginsburg’s separate writing in Randolph was a cited view, not a dissent in this case.

The Forum appointed independent arbitrators rather than itself deciding claims. They could not serve as its officers or directors, had duties of neutrality and conflict disclosure, and faced one peremptory strike per party and unlimited cause challenges. Coates’s speculation did not show these protections inadequate. Lee rejected substantive unconscionability.

On January 2, 2001, the court denied joinder and dismissal, abstention, and discovery, and granted Bank One’s motion to compel arbitration. It decided neither the financing allegations nor damages and did not expressly enjoin the state litigation. The assigned depositor problem changes the transaction to signature cards, account materials, and a statement notice; its outcome depends on those altered terms, not automatic transfer of the result in this satellite-credit case.
